Mission Pathways Pop-up & Stewards gathering · 24–26 August 2026

Eleven pathways walked in, one set of shared questions walked out.

Three days in a Wiltshire field. This is the whole arc — what was presented, what was argued over, what was decided, and what is still open. Skim it in five minutes, or switch on full detail and go as deep as you like.

In five minutes

What happened

If you read nothing else, read this.

Monday was 11 bodies of work presented back to back, each with twenty minutes and a live question. It was deliberately too much. Nobody could absorb it all. The point was to see it all at once, and what became visible, once you could, was how much of it rhymes.

Tuesday opened in 2050 with a museum of invented artefacts, then dropped straight into the two hardest questions in the room: how we construct our political and economic position, and what we build next. Seven open spaces followed, one of which — constructing politics — was the only session of the three days built purely to transfer craft, and the one people kept referring back to afterwards. By the afternoon the same finding had surfaced in four separate rooms: we are building several versions of the same thing, in parallel, without talking to each other about it.

Wednesday turned that outward and inward at once. Outward to the £11–13M that the Collaborative will allocate in November, and what a coherent Dm portfolio into it looks like. Inward to what stewardship actually means when the honest answer is that there is no externalised team coming to fix the gaps.

The single sentence version

The gathering found that Dm's biggest constraint is no longer ideas, funding, or talent. It is coordination between the things it is already doing, and the concentration of relationship-holding in a small number of people. Almost every action that came out of the three days is an attempt on one of those two.Inference

Monday

Eleven pathways, one shape

Every deep dive turned out to be some version of: many actors who need to act together, no institution that can make them, and no financing model that pays for the formation. Named directly in the tooling session as ‘large-scale multi-agent organising’.Said

Tuesday

Parallel, redundant, unspoken

‘I think we are doing too much parallel, redundant work. I can’t quite put my finger on where it is genuinely redundant… but I don’t think we’re having enough of these conversations.’Said The tooling, labs, pooled-funds and portfolio rooms all landed here independently.

Wednesday

The gaps have to be held by us

Stewardship was defined in the room as gap leadership: advocating for the unknown space between leadership spaces. The closing line of the fishbowl the day before: ‘There are no magical people coming to save us. We’re it.’Said

The shifts

Eight things that moved

Not summaries of sessions. These are the changes in position that happened across the three days — the places where the room ended somewhere different from where it started.

Shift one

‘Tool’ stopped being one word

The tooling session opened as a funding conversation and ended as a definitional one. Products, apps, protocols, services, knowledge assets, meta-tools and facilitation methods were all being called ‘tools’, which was making a shared decision impossible. Calvin’s reframe stuck: the value is the act of tooling and the epistemology embedded in it. The artefact is close to a MacGuffin. The agreed next step is an inventory that separates them.Said

Shift two

Climate to security is not a rebrand

The opening fishbowl argument. One position: language matters much less than underlying intent. If we need to drop the word climate to keep working on climate, drop it. The counter: moving from climate to security changes the boundary of the political object, and with it the portfolio, the strategy, and what counts as violence. Both were left standing. A working group was proposed to lay the tensions out rather than resolve them.Said

Shift three

Relationship-holding named as the craft

Wednesday’s clearest finding. Pathways do not come from bids; they come from relationships measured in years. The Camden work rests on trust seeded two years earlier at events. Newham traced back five years and a written reference. The most valuable money in the organisation’s history was described as ‘WhatsApp money’ — two £50k asks, sent as messages, that became Trees AI and Smart Commons. People can build pathways. What they cannot do is see where someone else’s relationships already run. Tuesday’s constructing-politics session is where that craft was actually taught rather than asserted.Said

Shift four

Evidence for futures became a buildable thing

What began as a support session for Civic Ledger turned into a taxonomy: fully transported evidence, partial compound evidence stitched into a chain, modelled extrapolation, and primary agent-based modelling. Plus a proportionality rule: do not build evidence that costs more than the decision it unlocks, the explicit lesson from Trees AI. Nobody in the room had seen this written down anywhere. It is now something Dm could publish.SaidInference on the publishing move

Shift five

Closing things is now on the table

Three separate provocations converged: a reflection on and audit of existing and previous labs; an enabling constraint that no new inquiry space opens until existing ones reach follow-through; and a minimum-viable-conditions blueprint so that anyone starting a unit knows what they are signing up for. The counter-position — self-audit, not collective audit, no invisible externalised committee — was accepted into the design.Said

Shift six

xCO became the centre of gravity, and that is now discussable

Set out plainly in the new-labs session note: xCO is currently the primary funding vehicle and nearly everything new is being seeded through it, with its own portfolio logic and its own spin-in trajectories. RZ is registered as an entity. The Ocean Studio is being designed for spin-in from the start. The open question — what is Dm then, if it becomes a capability provider to a group of spin-in entities — was named but not answered.Read

Shift seven

The Collaborative needs a Dm process, not 15 proposals

Last round Dm put in around 15 proposals and received roughly £300–400k of an £8M allocation. The critique from inside: it looked scattergun, it bottlenecked through one person, and it was assembled too late. For November the two stated criteria are pre-strategy work and planetary-scale coordination, each proposal needs one partner inside the Collaborative and one outside, and the bottleneck needs diversifying.SaidFigures approximate — recording unclear

Shift nine

The craft got taught, once, and it worked

One session was built purely to transfer craft rather than share work: a granular walk through how the Camden position was actually constructed, move by move, including the mistakes. Two people independently named it as the most useful thing they took away, and a third proposed making it a monthly format: dissect two pieces of work, in public, the same way. It is the clearest thing the three days produced about what pathway building actually consists of, and there is nothing structural yet to make it happen again.Said

Shift eight

Human-plus-machine got its first clear benchmark

The Madrid indicative portfolio — 17 impact chains, monetised value at risk to 2050 and 2100, 190-plus candidate interventions — was called the best example of human-and-machine work anyone had seen in Dm, by someone who had spent an earlier session voicing nervousness about how fast things were being built. The difference named: line-by-line human work with the model, not a prompt and a spreadsheet.Said

What now

The register

Everything the three days produced that someone has to pick up. Highlighted rows are the ones with a clock on them. Names are recorded only where someone named themselves or was named in the room. Anything else is left blank on purpose.

Read the ownership column carefully

An idea offered in a fishbowl is not a commitment. Where the transcript shows someone volunteering, it says so. Where it shows a suggestion nobody picked up, it says that too. If your name is here and you did not agree to this, the record is wrong and should be corrected before this circulates.

Moving now — the November clock is running

The Collaborative gathering is in November, decisions land around December, and the partner ideation sessions have already started.

Monday

Eleven deep dives

20 minutes each, roughly ten of presenting and ten of the room. Deliberately more than anyone could absorb. The full session-by-session harvest already lives in the Afterglow rooms. This is the one-line version, plus what each one is actually asking for.

01

Dm in Spain

What began as one line of work is now around 21 people touching Spain across adaptation, mitigation, food, justice, finance and governance. The framing was place rather than project. The finding was that a geography is now a real unit of Dm strategy.

Asks: act more intentionally in Spain; protect the liminal position while building recognition.

02

Homes That Don't Cost the Earth

Reframed from building homes to providing housing without constructing it. At least 30 UK local authorities could meet their annual targets inside the existing building stock. The initiative is designed so partners can buy a part rather than the whole.

Asks: cross-pollination on UK actors and EU relationships so pitches are not limited to one strand.

03

Camden Regenerative Food Systems

Move London's buying power — boroughs, schools, the NHS, large employers — to underwrite a nutrient-dense, civic-led food system. Camden is bought in and re-investing. The next move is other boroughs. The whole thing rests on relationships seeded two years ago.

Asks: resourcing the portfolio financially; how to hold soft power humbly.

04

Bioregions and RZ

RZ is now a registered spin-in: a fund plus a venture studio, working with Findhorn, South Yorkshire and Normandy on new allocation mechanisms. Alongside it the bioregions arc holds the tooling: a patterns database, workshop cards, a card game, and the European Headwater Flow Fund.

Asks: where the Tayside and Ebro Delta work sits as RZ separates out.

05

Cities, Resilience and Security

An honest account of the Net Zero Cities era: the hypothesis was that programmes would build deep city relationships, and that proved much harder than expected — but real trust now exists in Lund, Malmö, Madrid, Sheffield, Newham, Valencia and elsewhere. Funding will shrink; the relationships stay.

Asks: we chronically under-shared and under-published our insights.

06

Ladywood: 3º 2.0 and Retrofit Land Trust

The other end of the scale from bioregional allocation: one street of 41 houses, two homes moving toward community ownership, one abandoned factory becoming a neighbourhood square. What comfort standard do you design to when a heatwave, a drought and a cold snap are all live questions?

Asks: bring more of Dm's risk expertise into the place.

07

Many-to-Many and Beyond the Rules

Six years, 11 contract extensions with one funder, and a three-year proof of possibility that recently closed. The thesis: social agreement is not hard; converting it into contractual and legal structure without reverting to status-quo DNA is. That is where the deep-code work lives.

Asks: where does this trajectory go next — close, spin, or fold into learning systems?

08

Governing Together

Ontology first. Relational capacity is not mainly about how well people get on; it is a claim about what you can see and therefore design from. One hundred thousand people is not a hundred thousand units, it is the units and their interactions. Ask a council for its resilience strategy and it recites the plan; ask what actually happened and you learn something else.

Asks: make relationality a design input, not a value statement.

09

Next Economics

Two pathways six months ago; one is now unheld. Cornerstone Indicators are strongest in Sheffield and honestly weak at Findhorn. The tooling diagnosis — nothing is interoperable, so there is no end-to-end infrastructure, so no context agent, so no automation — produced Nomos, now live with a Scottish rivers trust.

Asks: the field-building strand is up for grabs. Who takes it?

10

Civic Ledger

Seven years from digitalising noise licensing in Camden to agreement infrastructure. Trust accumulates as evidence for future permissioning and deliberately does not convert into money. A pilot across three Korean jurisdictions; a demonstration app built in English so the rest of us could try it.

Asks: the coordination design cannot be machine-generated. What is the craft?

11

xCO

The renamed Civilizational Options Fund: a formation studio and capital platform that finances options before they are bankable. Frontier, Fortress, Field as the pitch that lands. An atlas of 115 systems. A staircase from £5M seeded to a £350M platform ask. Madrid as the worked example.

Asks: funders, talent in systemic accounting and metadesign, and the tools for large-scale organising. The room asked about risk and governance instead.

Before all of it

The opening circle

Two minutes each, no responses, 30 seconds of silence between speakers. Almost everyone answered with a pair rather than a hope and a fear. The most repeated hope: becoming an actual team rather than an aggregate. The most repeated fear: that we are good enough at diagnosis to spend three days diagnosing.

12 agreements came out of it — see below.

The twelve agreements, as adopted

Framed not as workshop hygiene but as behaviours this group carries out of the room and models to the rest of Dm for the next 6–12 months. Revisitable at any point.From the flipchart

1. Assume best intent; attend to impact.

2. Stay curious about each other's ideas for a question or two before bringing your own frame.

3. Invite conversations to pause when needed. All of us hold the space.

4. Yes/and; both/and — ‘I see your vantage point, and I have another view.’

5. Listen with your whole body. A sensory response is as valuable as an intellectual one.

6. Engage tension, don't indulge drama.

7. W.A.I.T. — Why Am I Talking? Be open to someone else speaking your truth.

8. Make space, take space — in that order.

9. Self-care and group care — in that order.

10. Lightness and fun. Remind ourselves of the privilege of being here.

11. Grace about our diverse experiences. What looks like anxiety may be the courage it took to speak.

12. Have real conversations. Embrace disagreement and find the fifth option. Stay kind; not nice.

One agreement was affirmed and never written up: stay energised to the end — sleep and alcohol as the critical factors nobody plans for. Worth deciding whether it is a thirteenth principle or something simply held in mind.

Tuesday

2050, two hard questions, six rooms

The longest and densest day. It began in a museum of the future and ended with four separate rooms arriving at the same diagnosis.

Dispatches from 2050

Everyone made an artefact from an imagined 2050 and presented it in character: a whale treaty drafted by a 17-member multi-species committee, a wampum belt encoding protocols with self-owning land, a coral immunity vaccine, the last passport ever issued, collective care accounts replacing pensions, a floppy disk, a bottle-cap bioregional key, a golden staircase with a plastic plant representing the historiography of getting here, and a non-extractive internet running on coral and algae.

Then the reframe that made it serious: ‘I don't think the things we've talked about are off reality. If this was the portfolio of Dm in 2027 at that scale, it would not be crazy — in fact it might be more appropriate to the problem space we're operating in.’Said The full harvest of that session is already written up.

The fishbowl: our political and economic position

20 minutes, gut reactions only, anyone can tap in. It ran long.

The opening question was blunt: should we play it safe-ish, or would Dm be unlocked by being radical? What followed was the most substantive disagreement of the three days, and it did not resolve.

The pragmatist case. Language matters far less than underlying intent. Some of Dm's most interesting work on civic economy happened under a government whose politics nobody in the room admires, because we brought a framing that worked. In Madrid, some of the people we want to work with will not be in a room together — if adjusting the language lets us work across all of them, adjust it. If we need to drop the word climate to keep working on climate, drop the word.

The counter. Moving from climate to security is not a language shift, it is a systemic worldview shift that changes what the portfolio looks like. If you take a security perspective the question becomes what are you securing — the individual, their future, or a future only possible if you secure the whole planet. These are conceptual moves that change the boundary of the political object, and therefore the strategy, the tools, and what counts as violence.

The distinctions that landed. Non-partisan but political — partisanship is the polarised, emotional field; being political is bringing intentions and values into a conversation about governing the city. Entering at Horizon One to get somewhere near Horizon Three, because you have to speak to someone where they are. And a plurality of identities: different virtual debit cards, one bank account, as long as the underlying purpose holds.

What was left unfinished. Three colleagues, not in the room, spent a long time trying to get a decision made about not working with certain cities and partners and never got one. The question put to the group — are we saying we want to take stances, and do we have a protocol for taking them — did not get answered.

‘We should be very wary of hanging ourselves up to particular language and making the language the object of our concern versus the underlying work.’
Day 2 fishbowl
‘These aren't just words. They are conceptual shifts that change the boundary of the political object.’
Day 2 fishbowl
‘We don't want to be partisan. We want to be non-partisan, but we want to be political — and those are two different things.’

Day 2 fishbowl

The fishbowl: what are our next labs and arcs

Everything proposed, in the order it came: a lab for theoretical and political construction; human consciousness and more-than-human comprehension; meaning-making; rapid optionality prototyping; a culture lab; media and communications; biomimicry and a non-extractive internet; a revived Foresight Studio; a capability lab oriented to actually building things rather than iterating on paper.

And then the pushback, which is the more useful half. Creating new labs for the sake of it was questioned on the grounds that it carries an internal cost in meaning, craft and professional identity as well as an external one — evolving and renaming can be the right move, and can also quietly erode what a team knows it is good at. Against that, an argument that the audit should be individual rather than collective: everyone continuously evaluating whether their own positions are viable, rather than a committee doing it to them.

Underneath the whole exchange, a distinction that stuck: we are neither a team nor a community of practice. We are a community of teams — and the question is how a community of teams organises itself.

The seven open spaces

Constructing politics — the tactics, in granular detail

Held by Indy, who framed it and then mostly stayed out of the way. Adam gave the Camden account. Ran in parallel with pooled funds.

The session everyone kept referring back to for the rest of the gathering, and the only one explicitly designed as craft transfer. The framing: the work we are trying to build — food systems, pooled cities, any mass multi-party endeavour — requires the active construction of the political engineering of its context, and that is a practice we are having to build. The instruction to Adam was unusual: go into the detail and the precision. What was the first document? What was the sequence of moves?

Set against a pattern from the pre-work: our work is becoming fast and sticky, and it moves off the back of existing relationships. Cold bids are not winning us anything at the moment.

How Camden actually happened

The relationships go back to Impact Hub days. People who were friends then are now in positions of power in the systems we want to operate in. On that basis Indy was invited in to provoke, more than once, and the provocation was specific: you need a devolved food partnership, all your food organisations need to come together, backed by the council but facilitated rather than run by it.

The two officers leading the food work on the ground did that well — and then, in Adam’s account, did a poor job of the next part. A diverse group was convened and given no coordination, no synthesis, no direction, and no conditions in which it could find its own direction. Meetings were chaired on the assumption that putting people in a room produces magic. It did not.

That gap is what Dm was brought into. Indy first, then Adam at the point it was crystallising, and the first £20,000 was to build an indicative portfolio — which meant being paid to go and talk to a large number of people on the ground. Tactically, what the council actually wanted was a way to pool capital into the partnership at a larger scale, with a large technology company acting as the golden carrot. So the first real question was whether Dm could structure a capital pool. The Growth Pot was then used to match-fund what the council put in, which lowered the risk for the officers carrying it internally.

The politics they had to work through

Named plainly: the politics of people not wanting their peers to succeed. One officer — the head of the food mission, sitting alongside the two doing the work — was initially resistant precisely because they were his peers. The generalisable observation: in councils you meet people whose job, as they understand it, is not to rock the boat, and who calculate that if others rock it and it goes wrong they look bad. The flip comes when you make them look good and they learn to trust you.

Above him sits the council sponsor with sign-off power — the relationship Dm has only recently formed, and who came to the workshop. The move that got there is the one worth keeping: internal relationships are only validated by horizontal ones. Talking to the businesses, the cooperative and the technology company built the credibility that let the council advocate inwards. You could not lobby inside; you had to go wide to earn the standing.

The mistake, in Adam’s own words

Working most closely with the most motivated officer on the ground meant sending things to her first — which annoyed her colleague, the mission head. ‘You learn where a line is by overstepping it.’ What followed was reading the signal and working out what that colleague actually needed, which turned out to be priority of information: to be in the know before others. Texting him on holiday to say what had just happened was enough.

The second admission, offered when Adam asked the room for failures: having opened a conversation with that same officer about joining Dm or being jointly employed, before understanding how exposed she was to the person who wanted to keep control of her. ‘A bit of a fuck-up — moving too quickly and over-promising too quickly in these contexts has been a thing for me.’ Named as a lesson the organisation has learned before.

Holding a hostile actor without going to war

One influential local actor has used the language of social justice to accumulate power and, on this account, to paralyse the people around her; she is the one who has called Dm a surveillance company. The fracture point was a conversation in which the future trajectory implicitly questioned whether her organisation would still be needed. The response was deliberate: keep the door fully open, never use the platform being built to weaponise against her, disagree openly, and simply deliver the effective process cleanly. Her peers have since come to Dm privately.

What is our role, exactly

Asked directly in the room. The answer had two halves. Dm’s shape gives you wriggle room early in a relationship, so the role has deliberately not been nailed down — but the intent has been declared: we intend to invest our own resource and crowd in others. And then a precision that was insisted on: we are not investing in them, we are investing in the mission and the portfolio together. Saying we are doing free work for Camden would change the power relation. The trajectory is a shared capital pool, and everyone involved knows it cannot sit inside the borough. The officers said so themselves: when you build this pot, do not build it in here.

Two moves on scale

Widen out early. Hold Camden too tightly and it becomes political capture by Camden, and they will not know how to let go. Turning it into a London conversation creates the internal competition dynamic that lets them move. The general rule offered: you start with one, you go to three, and the next trajectory may open anywhere across the three — going deeper down the one does not work.

Borrow authority. Peer confidence matters — officers meeting other boroughs’ officers — and so does political cover from someone with standing. Once a nationally recognised food-systems academic who advises central government said the work was good, it created a virtuous cycle of reference.

Alongside it, a competitive move: with a national funder deploying eight grants of around £4M into the food system, rather than partner with a would-be competitor and split one bid, they agreed to run the same theory of change in different geographies — on the reading that funders will back a bigger, bolder play.

Officers, not politicians

A few elected members came to the talks, but the work is happening among officers rather than elected members, partly because officers hold protected relationships with each other and bypassing them costs you. One counter-move: make it your business to meet the council’s chief executive early, to keep a wedge in the door and avoid being kept below. And then never use it. ‘You never go up to go down.’ Having the capability is what keeps the system honest.

Madrid, for contrast

The Madrid team drew the distinction sharply. In Camden the legibility and the appetite were already there and what was missing was directionality. In Madrid the risk is real but perceived differently by different actors, and there is no shared understanding that this matters — so the work has been building legibility first. A dinner before now would have been premature, because the conversations were not there.

The harder ask in Madrid: everyone in Camden was already interested in food. Heat is not these actors’ thing. They do not work well together, do not see each other as peers, and do not see themselves as sharing a mission — and the shift being asked for is from thinking individually within a mandate to thinking collectively. What makes it possible is the value-at-risk work, which changes the posture from we are a non-profit here to help solve the world’s problems to we are here to help you protect your assets, with numbers behind it. And it needs three to five people, not one, because no single person can hold those threads.

New York, Korea, Santiago, Berlin

New York. Everyone wants to work with the new administration, so the first meeting was hostile ground — 30 minutes, officials answering email in the background. It turned on a refusal: no short-term work, because transformation requires long-term partnership. What they asked for instead was a long-term learning partnership and a space to de-risk and experiment. The tactic underneath it is the one Indy generalised: grow your counterparty’s power. Dm is bringing influential directors into the room specifically to build the standing of the official it works with, so that mass engagement reads as co-governance rather than a branding exercise. And a second move that worked: saying honestly that we do not know how to do this at scale, and asking for 18 months to find out. That landed better than a ready-made offer — but you have to be confident enough to say it.

Korea. The same pattern from the other side — a civil servant being quietly supported, who has started translating Dm’s language into local political language unasked. And an honest blockage: the money is visibly moving toward technology-driven innovation, several meetings have happened, and what Dm brings to the table has not yet been legible enough to carry into the next meeting. Indy’s response: work back from their deep motives — personal, economic, risk — rather than importing ours.

Santiago. A regional government that reads Dm as free consultancy, with an election making them want something to show by December. The red line held in the room: we are not providing consultancy, we are building a public interest capital facility — which they cannot build internally anyway for taxation reasons. Keep the mandate clear and it is an alignment of mission rather than a service to their reality.

Berlin. A closed-room session with officials a week before the city elections, to sense the trends before deciding what the coalition is. Flagged in response: in most democracies officials cannot speak publicly in the weeks before an election, and will avoid private meetings too, because being referenced can cost them their job.

Do it with no expectation, or it becomes corruption

The strongest thing said in the session, and the condition on everything above. The conditional work — the introductions, the papers sent overnight, the funder connections — has to be done with no expectation of return. Otherwise you are manipulating the system rather than genuinely helping people advance their own reality.

Pooled funds and allocation futures

Hosted by Annette and Fang

The realisation that opened it: Dm is now running or co-designing at least six allocation vehicles — xCO, Heart Power, the Unfurling Fund, Headwaters and RZ, the Collaborative, and the internal Growth Pot — plus match funding and internal redistribution. Raising in one place and reallocating somewhere else is a genuinely new organisational capability, developed over about two years, with only light sharing between the people doing it.

Design questions that recurred across all of them: open call or invitation, and what invitation-only does to power; whether an institution should be built to dissolve on purpose once it has distributed; who holds accountability when it does; how to handle entangled interest when the people best placed to design an allocation process are also the people best placed to build the thing. The reframe offered: conflict of interest is the lazy answer — design firewalls and integrated interest instead, so someone can vouch for others but not for themselves.

The many-to-many contribution: many forms of value coded into the contract, so that if something goes wrong the mediation covers relational and reputational loss as well as financial, and considers who is best placed to absorb which kind.

Out of it: the Allocation Futures channel and comparison table.

Tooling fund

Hosted by Annette and Indy

The brief: xCO can seed the development of a tooling capability, focused specifically on organising very large multi-actor, multi-agent systems. The stated assumption — organising farmers in a bioregion the analogue way took one partner five years, and we have neither five years nor the hosting capacity, so something has to reduce the transaction cost of organising at scale.

What the room did with it was mostly definitional, and productively so. Is it a tool or a product? Self-serve or service-wrapped? Who is the user — the bioregion, the city, or us? The strongest observation came from the relationship side: what partners value first is the relief that someone has already thought the question through. The tool is the bonus.

Two honest constraints named. Building real multi-actor infrastructure means sensitive data, security protocols, maintenance, and a software team — that is not a side project. And going to cities to sell products has been tried and has not worked; the competition there is the large consultancies, not Silicon Valley.

Out of it: an inventory, a named tooling circle, and a genuine strategic choice still to make.

Indicative portfolio — Madrid heat

Presented by Oliver and Sofia

The most technically detailed session of the three days, and the one that drew the loudest applause. 17 impact chains derived from Spain's national risk assessment and downscaled to Madrid, each broken into hazard, exposure and vulnerability, with indicators, baselines and projections to 2050 and 2100 under two IPCC warming scenarios — then monetised into value at risk per year, by sector.

Against that sits a long list of 190-plus candidate interventions across building, street, neighbourhood and city scale, tagged by intervention type, which risk component they address, which impact chains they touch, which of seven demonstrator sites they suit, maturity horizon, and how they act on the risk — attenuate, multiply, transfer, or drive uptake.

What the room added: cascading and compounding effects that formal plans never capture, drawn from Chicago, Katrina, Australian bushfires and Greece; the need for human stories alongside monetised risk; a governance-of-governance layer with working groups by intervention type so the portfolio is not delivered by Dm; and the observation that this is market-making for the insurance sector, which is far ahead on flooding and nowhere on heat.

The framing that matters most: this is not a plan and not a product. It is a device that lets a coalition understand that something is possible, and a demand-construction tool. The portfolio will change drastically once Madrid's own actors prioritise.

Evidencing the futures

Working session with Eunji, Fang, Joost and Indy

Most of Dm's work sits outside the existing evidence base, because nothing like it has happened before. So the question becomes how you construct a credible argument about a future. Four modes were laid out, in descending order of borrowed confidence: transported evidence — this happened in another city, assume the context is similar, and it usually is not; partial compound — none of it has happened together but each component has, so link them into a chain and say this is likely; modelled extrapolation on top of that chain for one or two factors; and primary modelling from biophysics or thousands of agents.

Two rules came out of it. Only prove the link in the chain that is genuinely unproven — the longitudinal benefits of children's play are already established, so all you have to show is that a certain kind of space gets more children playing more often, or you create a burden of evidence on yourself for no reason. And keep the cost of evidence proportionate to the value of the decision it unlocks. The Trees AI post-mortem given in the room: the compute cost of getting to high resolution far exceeded what anyone would pay for that resolution.

The deeper move, for Civic Ledger and anything like it: stop trying to evidence the features and start evidencing the efficacy of the agreement — is it more resilient, does it hold volatility better, does it widen the option space — then work out what markets that efficacy addresses.

Securing urban futures

With Joost, Amelia, Indy, Prateek, Calvin, Max, Alicia and others

The context: European priorities shifted hard from climate to security and resilience, and once that frame arrives you cannot unsee it. Cities are where the risk lands and where citizens’ discontent lands, but cities are rarely in the room where resilience is decided. Three openings were named — the EU Critical Entities Resilience Directive forcing every government to designate critical infrastructure, NATO accession obligations in Sweden, and the new EU budget being negotiated toward 2028.

The systemic argument: cities have been optimised for efficiency, which means minimal storage of energy, water and food; global supply chains are open to climate disruption; and total war now means switching off a waste-to-energy system with hackers or disrupting fertiliser routes. That gives a portfolio unlike bunkers and shelters — registry infrastructure that cannot be weaponised if a state is captured, storage, distributed industrial production, permissioning infrastructure.

The strongest challenges came from inside the room. That the whole design is calibrated to Russia when Chinese influence undermines European cities legitimately, through purchase, long before anyone needs a bunker. That accepting the security framing means accepting conflict, competition and extraction as inevitable, which cuts directly against the narrative being run with Civic Square — so a vision has to be constructed alongside it. And that resilience and climate investment compete for literally the same steel, labour hours, budgets and coastal space.

Two things carried forward: use ‘tri-use’ — security, adaptation and economic — rather than the military term dual use; and treat this as a position with several options being explored, rather than committing to one city.

What new labs do we need

This one is summarised from the reviewed session note in the Circle, which is the source of record. Some of what was said in the room was paraphrased or removed at review, so the note is the version to work from and to quote.

The move that reframed it. The question was which new labs to create, and what is missing from the current portfolio. Within five minutes it had become a different question: rather than adjudicating what Dm’s labs should be, who is actually willing to build one? Unless someone in the room will build the culture lab, the room has no standing to say there should be one. The constructive half: as you build the thing you are actually interested in, name the enabling constraints you applied, and offer those as a model for other builders. Working out loud and demonstrating, rather than designing a frame and building afterwards.

What distinguishes a lab, a studio and an arc. A lab builds capabilities for external-facing work and does not resource itself — it goes into projects, the projects resource it, it comes back. That model is reported to be working. A studio is an internal learning space. Arcs are held tightly; labs are sites of intersection. Applied live, the consciousness work was reclassified as a studio rather than a lab, and Beyond the Rules — called a lab — is probably a transversal arc.

The resourcing test that follows. Whether a lab is viable is not a question of appetite but of whether the work already exists to fund it. Foresight and futures could revive on that basis today. A human consciousness lab could not, yet.

How things have historically started. Three routes: championing an idea until it accumulates internal buy-in, then external buy-in, partnerships and funding; gap-filling, where a missing frame is identified and something starts with roughly £20k and a scoping exercise; and — now seen as the most useful — a site of intersection, where something stops being a project because it was always working across other projects.

The blocker nobody has solved. If you show up to a shared learning space, where do you track your time? If your unit has no funded projects, attendance becomes citizenship time. There is no infrastructure in which leadership, nurturing teams and nurturing learning are valued and resourced.

xCO’s gravitational pull. All QCF funds sit under xCO, making it the only guaranteed resource other than European Commission funding. All project fundraising runs through it and very few pathways are being developed independently. It carries its own portfolio logic, and one studio is designed for spin-in from the outset with its own matrix and domains.

Three patterns worth keeping. The first Matrix already ran this experiment — labs were suggested, many are now dormant, and the ones people genuinely ran with, they ran with. Spare capacity is not spare capability; reading utilisation at book level produces a feeling of safety rather than actual safety. And units fail financially for governance reasons rather than commercial ones: a unit lead missing minimum requirements creates stress downstream that becomes an organisation-level unsustainability narrative, when the root cause is that the governance inside the unit was never set up. That is the sharpest argument in the session for a founding sandbox.

What had genuine agreement behind it

Nothing was formally decided — the conversation recognised itself as too small to clear anything. Three things carried agreement: position through leadership, meaning build the thing and then offer the constraints as a model rather than designing a system for others; a monthly content space where unit holders dissect two projects together, explicitly with no authority attached — not an order, not an audit body, which is what makes distributed self-audit possible without becoming collectivism; and minimum viable conditions at founding, framed as a floor rather than a gate.

Alongside them, two proposals: financial sustainability as a founding condition, and co-leadership as the default, on the grounds that the four domains every unit needs — strategic partnership, fundraising, people holding, and organisation — are too much for one person.

The closing question, and the most useful thing in the session. We have a lot of speaking — but where do we clear it? Conversations happen and do not land anywhere. The Stewards have enough permission to clear things, but it needs somewhere to land, with a rhythm and some general orienting devices. With a rhythm you can be both intentional and organic; the rhythm is the intentional part.

And one outcome of the pop-up itself, surfaced here. Mission Pathways has always been amorphous — a tri-weekly call, unclear membership, participation by interest and availability. This is the first time the group has been mandated as pathway builders in a way that makes it possible to tell someone what building a pathway takes, and who to talk to.

The tactics, written down

The constructing-politics session was the only one in the three days designed to transfer craft rather than share work. These are the moves it produced, in the form they were offered. Handbook §3 and §4. The underlying recording names officials in a partner council and should stay internal.

Provoke before you propose

Go in and say what the work is, at events and one to one, with clarity and without an ask. The provocation itself becomes the reason you are invited back, and it sets the direction they later pay you to define.

Get paid to build the indicative portfolio

The first £20k should buy the thing that changes what everyone thinks is possible — and buy you the reason to talk to everyone on the ground while you build it.

Go wide to get in

Internal relationships are only validated by horizontal ones. Build credibility with businesses, funders and lateral actors so the officers can advocate inwards on your behalf.

Grow your counterparty’s power

Actively build the standing and relationality of the official you work with — introductions, funders, visibility. Systemic generosity, because you need the field to move with you.

Read the love language

Everyone in the system needs something different. For one it was priority of information — being in the know first. You often find the line by overstepping it; the skill is reading the signal afterwards.

Honeypots are legitimate

A big name or a big pot that might come in is a tool for moving people through a phase. It can be parked later once the conversation has grown past it.

Construct hunger, then mandate

Desire construction first. Then transform the mandate, because their existing mandate is too small for the work. Then show what is possible on the other side. Then build the movement.

Never go up to go down

Meet the chief executive early so you cannot be kept below — and then never use it. Having the line open is what keeps everyone operating with integrity.

Start with one, go to three

Hold a single place too tightly and it becomes political capture. Widening to three creates the peer competition that lets the first one move, and the next opening may come from any of them.

Borrow political cover

One respected voice saying the work is good creates a virtuous cycle of reference. Peer confidence between officers does the same job laterally.

Keep the hostile actor in the room

Do not ostracise, do not weaponise the platform you are building, disagree openly, and deliver cleanly. Their peers will find you.

Trusted ears, then circles

Test the work with ten people you can be genuinely open with, and bring them in early. They open the second circle, which opens the third. Ten to a hundred in two or three iterations.

Invite wildcards

Put a few people in the room who have no obvious connection to the work. They generate side quests, and you become top of their mind.

Shared experience to shared endeavour

The dinner changed the relationships before the workshop changed the strategy. People experienced the future rather than being shown it.

Send the work we already have

Dm sits on hundreds of papers and reports. You can do work for people without doing any work — find the existing piece, frame it, send it, expect nothing.

Gift with no expectation of return

The condition on every move above. Without it, the same tactics are manipulation of the system rather than help. Named in the room as the line between craft and corruption.

Wednesday

Money, stewardship, and what we each offer

The day opened with an unplanned reflection that turned out to be the frame for everything after it. On Tuesday the group had been running a familiar strategy exercise; someone pointed out the process was not sequential; someone else showed the curiosity to stop and hear it; the facilitators took the risk of scrapping the plan and switching to a fishbowl. That exchange changed where the whole gathering went. The point made on Wednesday morning: this adaptive capacity is exactly what organisations render invisible, and social systems cannot be built like buildings, because the bricks and the mortar and the location all change while you are building.

The Collaborative, and November

The systemic action collaborative now has around 27 partner organisations, up from about 12. Roughly £11–13M will be allocated after the November gathering. Two funder pots behave differently: one large allocation is geographically bounded to the Global South, and a second, smaller pot is unbounded and follows whatever the collective chooses.

The internal critique of last time was frank. Around 15 proposals went in, which looked scattergun. The portfolio as a whole was assembled from projects people already wanted funded rather than from a strategy. Almost all the information passed through one person. Dm received roughly £300–400k of an £8M allocation, most notably a large shared bioregions position.

The two criteria proposed for this round: fund work that sits ahead of a foundation's strategy — because once a foundation has a strategy it goes direct to organisations, so the Collaborative's value is in the window before that — and fund work that coordinates civic action at planetary scale, which is becoming the second source of value as geopolitics fractures.

The most careful part of the conversation was about the Global South allocation and the risk of a group of people in Europe deciding what happens in India or Ghana. The position taken: be narrow, do not touch a geography without a real partner on the ground, and where there is one, route capital as investment rather than grant, because foreign grant money is the standard way work gets discredited.

Stewardship, defined

17 Dm Stewards in total, in sub-circles: Mission Pathways, People and Capabilities, and Org Design and Structure. 14 were in the room, alongside eight pathway builders who are not stewards.

The definition that landed was narrower and more useful than ‘leadership’: stewardship is gap leadership — advocating for the unknown space between the leadership spaces, and stepping in when something goes wrong or the money is not there. It was previously held informally by a few people. The analogy offered alongside it: stewards create the soil in which other forms of leadership grow.

What the pathway builders asked for, in order of how often it came up: help handing pathways over without losing the relationship or putting personal reputation at risk; visibility of where fertile long-term relationships already exist, so newer people are not starting from their own past networks; mentorship on unfamiliar funding cultures; feedback loops that capture what happened when a pathway converted or failed; and a bank of backing assets ready for the moment an opportunity arrives.

The most quoted craft insight of the three days

The return on cold bids is low, because bids work when the other party already knows what they want and we work outside what is deemed known. What works instead is creating the field for work to come to us. The worked example given: a £35k piece of work on the future of cities became a roughly £10M programme, which set the ground for a partnership allocation an order of magnitude larger again. That is an 18–24 month pathway, and it requires running on predictive foresight rather than reacting to a gap in September.

Alongside it, the counter-nuance: several successful bids were formal tenders, but never cold — they responded to briefs shaped in relationship, sometimes across more than five years. The red thread is relationality, not the absence of bidding.

The closing circle: what I offer, what I take

Everyone named one thing they are offering the group and one thing they are taking away. The offers are a live directory — this is the list to come back to when you need something.

Offered

  • Sitting in the questions, and camaraderie
  • A focus on detail and production rigour
  • Help to anyone who asks, no conditions
  • A warm and positive spirit, and a door that stays open
  • Unwavering belief that we will find a way together
  • Building the CRM luck generator, and pushing that work forward
  • Renewed energy
  • Undefined design conversations
  • Championing and simplifying what everyone else is doing
  • A bouncing board for ideas, fears, frustrations and joys
  • Calm
  • Structures and conditions that create density of insight
  • Policy, government, EU and city translation — how to land a theoretical idea at government level
  • Running fast at a couple of things to see where it goes
  • An editorial eye and some off-colour humour
  • Portfolio alignment across the organisation
  • The tooling discussion from the city transition side, plus deep empathy and problem-solving joy
  • A daring fellow explorer, in civic spaces and capital places
  • Boundless energy and hacking the ambition of the work upward
  • Methodological and technical rigour on the production side
  • Curiosity, and deep work together
  • Honesty, Spain connections, and a call whenever it helps

Taken

  • Camaraderie, and being in it together
  • More momentum in a similar direction
  • Legitimacy, and a mandate as a group
  • ‘We are not alone — six of us doing something in parallel, and we can do it shoulder to shoulder’
  • A bigger sense of what is possible
  • Hope, from the density of intelligence in the room
  • Awareness of what everyone is doing, which reading the website never gave
  • Specific insight into how the politics of each pathway got built
  • Inspiration from the range of leadership styles present
  • ‘We are finally learning the lessons the universe keeps teaching us’
  • A sense of collective possibility
  • Lightness — named as the thing least taken for granted coming in
  • A new family
  • Michelle's voice in my head: who is going to do this? We are.
Threads

Ten things that ran through all three days

These are cross-sections, not summaries. Each one appeared in at least three separate sessions without anyone planning it.Grouping is analytical

Thread 01

We are building several versions of the same thing

Multiple tooling stacks on adjacent, similar, not-always-the-same problems of multi-actor organising. Named in the fishbowl, then independently confirmed in the tooling room, the pooled funds room and the labs room. The stated root cause: labs have been operating with very low coordination between them, so a relationship-holder cannot tell a partner what the rest of the system knows.

Thread 02

Relationship-holding is the craft, and it is concentrated

Partnerships are among Dm’s biggest assets, people are the holders of those assets, and relationship holding is the craft. And it is distributed across too few people, invisible in the accounts, and most fragile at handover. The gap is not capability, it is sharing.

Thread 03

Allocation is being designed in six places at once

xCO, Heart Power, the Unfurling Fund, Headwaters and RZ, the Collaborative, the internal Growth Pot — plus match funding and internal redistribution. Similar design questions in each; almost no shared learning until Tuesday. It now has a name and a channel.

Thread 04

Nobody owns closing

Dormant studios, unheld pathways, units that die with their originators, and an explicit worry about creating new labs to stay relevant while quietly destroying internal meaning and craft. Three separate mechanisms were proposed. None was adopted.

Thread 05

Internal legibility and external legibility are different problems

A framework that helps a team understand itself can actively harm the work externally — the same underlying property work reads completely differently to a Scottish government, an Indigenous rights foundation, and a housing developer. Hence tactical fluidity, plurality of identities, and a deliberate reluctance to be pinned down.

Thread 06

Evidence is the bottleneck, not the idea

Every pathway hit the same wall in a different form: the funder, the city, the investor, the civil servant all need a reason to believe. The response that emerged is a craft — construct chains of argumentation, borrow what is already proven, and only pay for the evidence you actually need.

Thread 07

Risk is the entry language now, everywhere

Heat risk in Madrid, security risk in Warsaw and the Baltics, climate risk in Ladywood, food-system risk in Camden, systemic risk in the Collaborative pitch. And a caution running alongside it: risk is a point of view, not a universal — a pound of risk against a pound of wealth is not the same trade as a pound against eight hundred million.

Thread 08

The machine changed the work, unevenly

The strongest praise and the clearest nervousness in the same three days. What separated them: the Madrid work went line by line with the model rather than accepting output; the coordination design in Civic Ledger was found to be something a model cannot do for you; and the most interesting proposal was to make an LLM learning infrastructure the first thing we set up with a new partner.

Thread 09

Legitimacy has geography

A clear line drawn about where Dm should and should not work, and how capital should move when it does. Alongside it, a lived account of what a captured state does to foreign-funded work, and a real fear that the countries where things cascade first are the ones treated as expendable.

Thread 10

The group prefers propositions to processes

Almost every time a process was proposed, someone converted it into a proposition someone would hold. No externalised audit team. No committee to approve new units. Self-audit rather than collective audit. The pattern is consistent enough to be a design constraint for anything built out of this gathering.

A direct answer

The seven stewardship gaps, tested against the transcripts

Sophia posted seven areas where there may be useful leadership gaps for the Mission Pathways Stewards to tend, and asked whether it feels right and what is missing. Here is what the recordings actually support, and three things the list does not yet cover.

The proposed gapWhat the three days evidenceRead
Strategic relationship holdingThe single most supported item. Every worked example of a successful pathway traced back to a relationship of two to five years. The most valuable money the organisation ever received came through trusted messages, not proposals. Newcomers said explicitly they can see something three years out but have no way to know where fertile ground already exists.Strongly evidenced
Pathway handoversNamed independently by three people, and identified in project finance as the consistent point where things go wrong. The nuance added: handover puts personal reputation at risk as well as the organisation’s, so people hold pathways back rather than pass them on when they cannot see who would take them.Strongly evidenced
CoherenceEvidenced, and sharper than the word suggests. Coherence here means something sharper than narrative. We are doing parallel, possibly redundant work without the mechanisms to notice it. The November portfolio is the immediate test case.Evidenced, and urgent
Positioning and authorshipEvidenced and unresolved — this was the hardest conversation of the three days. The Healthkeepers pattern offers a shape that avoids a central approval system: a working group, a standards layer, and a live response team.Evidenced, open
Building the craftEvidenced, with one correction: the craft the room kept naming was relationship-holding itself, plus evidencing futures and clean handovers. Political framing was requested by newer colleagues in a specific form — role-play, use cases, what to say and what not to say.Evidenced
Backing assetsEvidenced, with a specific and modest first ask: a two-pager per pathway so colleagues can put each other forward. Also a general deck and a set of stories. The version from the room: without one, I cannot help you.Evidenced, easy start
Learning infrastructureEvidenced, with a concrete design: two feedback loops, one at pathway conversion or definitive failure, one at project end against the original thesis. Plus effort-level and relationship-depth data. Plus the tooling and allocation inventories already committed to.Strongly evidenced

What the list does not yet cover

Three gaps surfaced repeatedly and do not map onto any of the seven.Inference from the transcripts, offered for testing

Deciding what to close

Every version of this — audit, enabling constraint, sunsetting process, minimum viable conditions — was raised, argued over, and left without an owner. The stewards may be the only group that can hold it without it becoming a committee, precisely because the room rejects committees.

The shape of Dm alongside xCO

Named plainly and then dropped for time. If most new work is seeded through one vehicle with its own logic, and entities keep spinning in and out, the question of what Dm is — and what core funding it needs — is upstream of everything else on the list.

The resourcing signal loop

A clear signal was given that the forecast for the rest of the year is not strong, and that pathway activity and forecast gaps need to reach the stewards early. There is a bridge to build between project finance and pathway building that nobody currently walks.

Unresolved

Eight tensions still standing

Held rather than settled. Listing them is more honest than pretending to a convergence that did not happen.

Language pragmatism against conceptual integrity

Drop the word to keep the work, versus the word is the work because it changes the boundary of the political object. Both positions were held by people with strong track records.

One identity against a plurality of them

A stronger, clearer Dm brand that speaks for itself, or several faces on one underlying purpose. The room noted that when the faces clash, partners read it as distrust.

Collective audit against self-audit

An enabling constraint on new creation, or everyone continuously evaluating their own positions with no invisible committee. The counter to collectivism won the argument; nothing replaced it.

Team against community of practice

A team builds collective agency toward outcomes; a community of practice builds individual self-efficacy. The proposed third option — a community of teams — is a name, not yet an operating model.

Bespoke depth against diffusion

High-contact relational work with 15 partners, or tools that reach a thousand people we have no contact with. The impact theory requires diffusion; the quality comes from proximity.

The security frame against the regenerative narrative

Using security logic to build systemic civil resilience, while running a parallel argument that climate transition plans represent a new form of extraction. Accepting one frame may quietly concede the other's premise.

Hiring capability against growing it

Whether Dm is an organisation that teaches. One position: hire who you need. The counter: whoever you hire will eventually exhaust what they know, and nothing is being cooked. Not settled; one participant chose to demonstrate rather than argue.

Speed against depth

Named in the opening circle as the balance the group might not land, and it recurred every day. Horizon Three was described as roughly six months away; the built environment moves in decades.

Lore

Vocabulary that entered the room

Terms that were coined, borrowed or sharpened during the three days, and are now in circulation. Worth holding consistently if we want them to travel.

Community of teams
Neither a team nor a community of practice. The proposed third answer to how Dm organises.
Gap leadership
What stewardship actually is: advocating for the unknown space between leadership spaces, and stepping in when something breaks.
Tri-use
Security, adaptation and economic value in the same investment. Coined in the room to escape ‘dual use’, which is a military term.
Allocation Futures
The working name for everything Dm is doing on reallocation design, and now a channel.
The luck generator
The relational practice that makes a pathway appear years later. Not a metaphor for chance — a description of a method.
WhatsApp money
Trust-based, low-friction funding asked for and granted in a message. Named as the most valuable money the organisation has ever received.
Integrated interest
The alternative to conflict of interest. Design firewalls so people can vouch for others but not themselves, rather than excluding the people best placed to build.
Butterfly institution
An institution created with its own dissolution designed in, so that it cannot accumulate power beyond its purpose.
Enabling constraint
A deliberate limit that makes better work — no new inquiry spaces until the existing ones reach follow-through.
Meta tools
Parametric tools with enough range to be localised in context, rather than narrow products. Proposed as where Dm already is.
Transported evidence
Evidence borrowed wholesale from another context. The weakest of the four modes, and the most commonly used.
Pre-strategy funding
The window before a foundation forms a strategy. Named as the Collaborative's real value, since once a strategy exists funders go direct.
Middle powers
Nations able to project at planetary scale but vulnerable to planetary risk. Proposed as the geopolitical alternative to dominion by great powers.
Cognitive and cultural security
Preferred to ‘counter-misinformation’, because whoever defines misinformation holds the power. Changes the portfolio from countering to redesigning the media environment itself.
Risk memory
What memory of crisis a city holds — which may bear little relation to its actual exposure.
Minimum viable conditions
What has to be true before someone starts a new unit. Explicitly not an approval gate.
The fifth option
Not this, not that, not a hybrid — a move that makes the context of the first two obsolete. Adopted in the twelfth agreement; not yet used on anything.
Luck generation
Named in the session and immediately corrected: it is not luck, it is continuous seeding forward. Sending someone the thing they need, with no expectation, years before it matters.
Systemic generosity
Actively growing your counterparty’s power and relationality, because you need the field to move in line with you.
Synthetic mandate construction
Transforming someone’s official mandate, because the mandate they have is too small for the work. One of four moves named as the pattern underneath the tactics.
Honeypot
A big name or a big pot that might come in, used to move a system through a phase, and parked once the conversation has grown past it.
Trusted ears
The ten people you can be genuinely open with. Test the work on them, bring them in early, and they open the second and third circles.
Side quests
What wildcards invited into a room produce. People with no obvious connection to the work who become advocates because they saw you operate.
Never go up to go down
Meet the chief executive early so you cannot be kept below, and then never use the line. Holding the capability is what keeps everyone honest.
Frontier, Fortress, Field
The xCO pitch. People fund expansion beyond constraints and self-protection under threat; so why not the foundations that make every other future possible?
Factory of danger
A mishearing of ‘a factor of danger’, immediately adopted. The best accidental coinage of the week.

How to read this, and what needs checking

Evidence tags

Said spoken in a recorded session, cross-checked between the two parallel recordings where both exist.

Read from a document in the pack — decks, the reference sheet, the wishlist, the flipchart photographs.

Inference reasoning across sources. Mine, not the room's. Argue with it.

Unverified heard but not confirmed — a name, a figure, an attribution the recordings do not settle.

Method

Photographs. 27 images from the pack and from colleagues’ phones. Several show identifiable people at work, which is fine internally and worth a second thought before anything travels further.

48 files: 32 unique session records totalling about 181,000 words, plus parallel voice-memo recordings used for cross-checking, eight decks and 36 photographs. Every Monday session and most of Tuesday and Wednesday were captured twice, on a speaker-diarised recorder and an undiarised one.

Where the two recordings disagree, the diarised version is used and the discrepancy noted. Where both are unclear — which happens most often with numbers and proper nouns — the item is tagged unverified rather than smoothed over.

Those are parts of the stewardship fishbowl, the India briefing, and the constructing-politics session in the Collaborative fishbowl.
